title: No Sewer? Your Yard Is the Treatment Plant #shorts
summary: More than 1 in 5 US households use septic or small cluster systems. Solids sink, grease floats, the liquid flows to a drain field and the soil removes bacteria and viruses; tanks are pumped every 3-5 years (US EPA).
tags: how does a septic system work
sources: More than one in five households in the US depend on individual septic (decentralized) systems or small community cluster systems; solids settle to the bottom as sludge, oil and grease float to the top as scum, the liquid wastewater (effluent) exits to the drainfield; the tank is a buried, water-tight container of concrete, fiberglass or polyethylene (US EPA, Learn About Septic Systems / How Septic Systems Work, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-septic-systems-work

In the drainfield the wastewater percolates into the soil, which naturally removes harmful coliform bacteria, viruses and nutrients (US EPA, How Septic Systems Work): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-septic-systems-work

Inspect at least every three years; tanks are typically pumped every three to five years; only flush human waste and toilet paper; keep out grease, wipes, diapers, coffee grounds and household chemicals (US EPA, How to Care for Your Septic System, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-care-your-septic-system

Maintenance about $250 to $500 every three to five years; replacing a failed conventional system costs between $5,000 and $15,000 (alternative systems more); more than four billion gallons of wastewater are dispersed below the ground every day; a malfunctioning system can cause groundwater contamination that can spread disease (US EPA, Why Maintain Your Septic System, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/why-maintain-your-septic-system

scenes.narration: More than one in five US homes flush into their own yard.
The flush goes into a buried tank. Solids sink, grease floats, and the water in the middle flows out under the lawn.
Then the soil does the cleaning. It filters out bacteria and viruses as the water soaks down.
The catch: the sludge stays. It has to be pumped out every {3|three} to {5|five} years.
